tagline.text: A volcano trek up South Cotabato's highest peak, sacred to the B'laan

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱1,000–3,000 (permit, guide and transport, per person for 2 days and 1 night)

children.text: The highest active volcano in South Cotabato is a cone-shaped mountain you can see from General Santos all the way to Koronadal. From Barangay Kablon in Tupi you climb a forest trail to a summit with views of Mount Apo and the Daguma Range in a two-day, one-night trek.
Mount Matutum is a stratovolcano in Tupi, South Cotabato, and the highest peak in the province. Sources give its elevation as anywhere from about
to
. The base is about
25 km
across, so the round cone silhouette is visible over a wide area, from General Santos to Koronadal City. Tupi, known for its pineapple plantations, is the starting point for the climb.
Geologically it is classified as an active volcano. The summit crater is about
wide and is breached by three gorges, and its floor is covered by dense forest about

deep. A phreatic eruption on March 7, 1911 is suspected but has not been confirmed. Hot springs are known at Acmonan and Linan to the west of the mountain. All active volcanoes in the Philippines lie on the Pacific Ring of Fire. A Philippine hiking site rates it 5 out of 9 in difficulty, trail class 3, a "minor climb" comparable to Mount Makiling climbed from the UPLB College of Forestry. The time required is 1–2 days, with 4–6 hours to the summit. The challenge is less steep rock than a long climb and a damp forest trail, so managing your schedule and water matters more than raw fitness. Smaller volcanic edifices called Landayao, Tampad and Albulhek lie to the west of the crater and Magolo to the north, and the area belongs to the Hamiguitan Range.

The whole mountain is a protected landscape, and its forest is said to hold 110 plant species and 57 animal species. It is known as home to the Philippine eagle and the Philippine tarsier, and many B'laan Indigenous families live at the foot of the mountain. The mountain is sacred to the B'laan, so it is important to follow your guide's instructions and respect sacred places.

The city of Tupi manages the climb as ecotourism. Before you go up, you get permission from the Tupi tourism office and hire a guide and porter, and every climber plants one seedling in a designated area. The local motto is "Amyak Maleh Matutum" ("climb and plant Matutum"). From the summit you can see 360 degrees over General Santos, Koronadal and Polomolok, with Mount Parker to the northwest, Mount Apo to the northeast and the Daguma Range.

The summit has a viewdeck ringed by a metal railing and a marker that explains the mountain's history. General Santos, Koronadal and Polomolok spread out below, and on clear days you can also see Mount Apo, Mount Parker and the Daguma Range.
The summit is said to be suitable for camping. On a two-day trip, many hikers enjoy the summit evening and the next morning's sunrise in quiet.
The roughly
3–4 hours
from Camp 1 to the summit pass through mountain forest hung with vines and moss. It is a damp, shady forest where you walk among moss and vines.
The first part of the walk from Barangay Kablon follows an open trail through rolling hills, fields and plantations. After about
1 hour
you reach Camp 1, which is the forest entrance and the only listed water source.
Each climber plants a seedling in a designated area. The seedling is described as costing about ₱10, and it becomes a pleasant ritual that records your climb.
The summit crater is a forested crater about
wide, split by three gorges. The scenery, with volcanic terrain overlapping tropical rainforest, can be appreciated even by beginner hikers.
B'laan villages lie at the foot of the mountain, and local residents often serve as guides and porters. Walking while listening to your guide is the best way to understand this mountain.

items.title: Two days, one night with summit camp
items.subtitle: Kablon, summit and descent

children.text: Leave General Santos or Koronadal for Tupi by bus or van.
Arrive at Kablon Crossing and switch vehicles to reach the Sitio Glandang jump-off.
Register at the tourist guard house or DENR office at the jump-off and confirm your guide and porters.
Start trekking and walk about 1 hour along the open trail between rolling hills and fields.
Reach Camp 1. Have lunch and refill your water.
Enter the forest trail and climb about 3–4 hours to the summit.
Reach the summit. Enjoy the sunset and evening views, then camp.
The next morning, watch the sunrise, eat breakfast and break camp.
Start the descent, return to the jump-off around noon, and in the afternoon take a bus back to General Santos, Koronadal or Davao.

These times are a suggested schedule from one hiking guide site and will vary with your pace and the weather. The same site says a day hike from Koronadal or General Santos is also possible, but check in advance whether you can get down before sunset.
Leave General Santos or Koronadal for Tupi on the earliest ride available. An early start is the key.
Go from Kablon Crossing to Sitio Glandang, register, and agree on the plan with your guide and porters.
Start trekking and refill water at Camp 1 about 1 hour later.
Expected arrival at the summit. Take in the view and eat lunch. Use the 4–6 hours reported in sources to estimate your arrival time.
Do not linger; start down. It is safer to descend the forest trail before afternoon storms arrive.
Return to the jump-off and catch a bus on the main road. Confirm with your guide that you will arrive before dark.
This day plan is an example that spreads out the claim by a hiking guide site that a day hike is possible. A two-day trip is safer depending on your fitness and the weather.
The easiest way is to fly from Manila to General Santos International Airport (GES). Check the latest flight schedules.
From the airport, go into General Santos and take a bus to Tupi.
Take a bus or van toward Tupi from General Santos or Koronadal and get off at Kablon Crossing. The mountain lies about 30 km north of General Santos, and it can also be reached from Koronadal.
There is no verified source for exact fares or schedules, so ask at the terminal.
From Davao, take a bus toward General Santos or Koronadal and continue to Tupi; after the climb, buses in the same direction are described as returning to Davao. Check the travel time locally.
From Kablon Crossing to the Sitio Glandang jump-off you travel by vehicle. Use a motorcycle or a chartered ride and negotiate the fare.
After the descent, return to the main road and take a bus to General Santos, Koronadal or Davao.
Staying in Koronadal or General Santos the night before makes the early start much easier. One guide plans the day around reaching Kablon Crossing at about 9 AM.

In the dry season there are fewer rain clouds, the trail is less muddy and the summit views are clearer. One travel guide gives the dry season as December–May and another as November–May, so sources differ; check the weather yourself before you leave.
A schedule that reaches the summit early, before the clouds build up, gives the best views. In the rainy season, expect afternoon storms and muddy trails.

Summit views are clearest early in the morning. Sources give the dry season as January–March, December–May or November–May, and one marks May as the wettest month, so be sure to check the forecast just before you go.

Overnight stays during the climb are mainly summit camping. Bring a tent, sleeping bag, rain gear and insect repellent, and pack plenty of food and water. The guide advises about 3 liters of water per climber, refilled at Camp 1.
After the climb, it is easiest to stay and eat in General Santos or Koronadal. Tupi is known as a pineapple-growing area. Look up restaurants and lodging in each city.
On the mountain you must carry your own cooking gear and fuel and bring all trash back down. Pack simple food for the summit dinner and the next morning's breakfast.
Contact the Tupi tourism office before you leave to confirm permits, guides and the latest rules.
Starting at dawn and reaching the summit before clouds build up gives much better views.
Be sure to bring rain gear and insect repellent. The forest is damp montane forest, and rain protection and repellent are recommended.
Carry about 3 liters of water per person and refill at Camp 1.
Take part in the seedling planting and plant only in the designated place.
At B'laan sacred places, follow your guide's instructions and be careful with photography and noise.
A waterproof pack cover and spare socks make wet forest trails more comfortable.
Confirm your onward transport before and after the climb.
If your schedule is tight, a summit camp over two days and one night is easier than a day hike.
Ask the tourism office about guide and porter fees in advance, and do not renegotiate at the jump-off. One trip report says a group lost time renegotiating with porters there.
This mountain is classified as an active volcano. Entry rules and local security conditions can change, so be sure to check with the Tupi tourism office and the latest announcements.
Do not enter without a permit; climb with a guide.
The forest trail is damp and slippery, and weather can change quickly, so bring rain gear and warm layers.
Water is hard to find after Camp 1. Fill up fully and ration it.
Safety is generally described as assured, but it may be a concern for some travelers, so check the latest information.
Respect the B'laan's sacred places and leave no trash.
If you do not agree on fees with your guide or porter beforehand, negotiation at the entrance can take a long time. Ask the tourism office first.
The gateway city about
30 km
south of the mountain, with an airport. See the city entry for the latest transport and lodging information.
A highland lake town southwest of the mountain, known for T'boli culture and waterfalls. It is a good follow-up after the climb.
The volcanic lake of Mount Parker, seen to the northwest from the summit. Plan it for a different day, and check the latest announcements for trekking and camping information.
The highest peak in the Philippines, visible to the northeast from the summit.
